overview: This file brings together a January 1938 consular despatch about Japanese colonial authorities’ refusal to permit Harvard doctoral researcher Paul King Benedict to conduct anthropometric and social research in Taiwan and four enclosures arising from the Second Stewart Psycho-Ethnographic Expedition to Koto-sho (modern Orchid Island) in 1936–1937. The enclosures—E. R. Leach’s answers to a police questionnaire, statements by Kilton R. Stewart and Nancy Grasby, and Grasby’s lengthy newspaper report—describe the Indigenous Yami people, the expedition’s research into dreams and psychology, and the island’s environment and social customs. They repeatedly praise Japanese colonial administration, while the covering despatch reveals official anxiety about foreign research into relations between colonizer and colonized and about describing Taiwan’s population as Chinese.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Paul King Benedict’s proposed anthropological studies in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports the Taiwan Government-General’s refusal to allow Paul King Benedict to undertake anthropometric and social research among Taiwan’s population.
subfiles.summary: Benedict arrived in Taiwan after war conditions frustrated his proposed fieldwork in China and sought to study communities beginning with Tamsui. Foreign-affairs official Choji Koshimura warned that research would inevitably touch the politically sensitive relationship between rulers and ruled, cited problems caused by the earlier Stewart expedition, and objected to Benedict’s description of Taiwanese residents as Chinese rather than Formosans and Japanese subjects. Authorities ultimately refused permission despite proposals that Benedict affiliate with Taihoku Imperial University and submit his notes for inspection. Benedict departed aboard the Hongkong Maru for Hong Kong, intending to seek permission in French Indochina and possibly the Philippines.

subfiles.title: E. R. Leach’s replies to a police questionnaire on Koto-sho
subfiles.about: Answers official questions about the expedition’s conditions, psycho-ethnographic research, the Yami people, and Japanese colonial policy.
subfiles.summary: Leach praises police help, describes collecting Yami dream narratives and testing symbolism via hypnosis, notes Batan cultural ties, calls Yami society advanced 'Late Neolithic,' warns against disruptive 'civilizing' but commends Japan's gradualist administration and schooling.

subfiles.title: Kilton R. Stewart’s statement on the Koto-sho expedition
subfiles.about: Expresses gratitude for official assistance to the expedition and praises Japanese policy toward the Yami.
subfiles.summary: Stewart thanks officials for securing permission, housing, and interpreters, depicting the Yami as a healthy, democratic community whose culture survived under Japanese rule, closing with emphatic approval of colonial policy.

subfiles.title: Nancy Grasby’s comments on her visit to Koto-sho
subfiles.about: Records Grasby’s appreciation of official assistance and her impressions of relations between the Yami and Japanese authorities.
subfiles.summary: Grasby calls her role secretarial, thanks Taihoku officials and guide Yuzuriha, praises administration for not overturning Yami traditions, and commends available medical services.

subfiles.title: Nancy Grasby’s Taiwan Nichi Nichi report on Koto-sho and the Yami
subfiles.to: Readers of the Taiwan Nichi Nichi
subfiles.about: Presents an extended popular ethnographic description of Koto-sho, Yami society, and the Stewart expedition’s research.
subfiles.summary: Grasby surveys Koto-sho’s geography, geology, vegetation, wildlife, settlements, and malaria, then describes Yami political organization, marriage, landholding, gender relations, birth customs, crafts, food, music, poetry, and art. She represents the Yami as peaceful, independent, democratic, and culturally stable, while praising Japanese officials for limited interference, schooling, policing, and medical care. The report concludes with information on Stewart, Leach, Trevor, the expedition’s mental testing and data collection, and its claim that Yami test results were comparable to those of the American children on whom the tests had been standardized.

interest: Shows constrained anthropology in colonial Taiwan, contrasting rejected Benedict fieldwork with favorable Yami-expedition assessments of Japanese rule.
